newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Politicians differ on Bulgaria economic tactics.
newsitem.headline: Politicians differ on Bulgaria economic tactics.

text.p: Bulgaria's opposition and ruling ex-communists see radical reform and implementation of a strict monetary regime as the solution to the country's grave economic crisis but remain far apart on tactics.

"What is needed to put together an IMF programme is a government to negotiate with, a parliament to pass the laws and national consensus on the policies," International Monetary Fund Sofia representative Franek Rozwadowski told reporters.

Speaking after a meeting with new president Petar Stoyanov, Rozwadowski said "the economic situation in Bulgaria is extremely grave and extremely dangerous, and whatever the solution of political problems, it is important that the economic problems be dealt with as soon as possible."
As daily rallies entered their third week on Tuesday the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) remained adamant on their demand for early elections.

UDF chairman Ivan Kostov told a news conference that if early elections were held in March, the new parliament would adopt the legal amendments needed for the implementation of a currency board in April and enable its introduction in May.
The IMF proposed the introduction of a currency board in November as a last resort to haul the country from the brink of debt default and stabilise the collapsing national currency.
The lev traded around 760 to the dollar on Tuesday, compared to 70 a year ago.

The Fund had begun talks with the outgoing Socialist government, which resigned on December 21, on the implementation of the currency board system which severely curbs financial powers of the government and the central bank.
Talks were expected to be completed after parliament approved a new Socialist government by mid-January.
The Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP), composed largely of ex-communists, has offered elections by the end of the year and a second Socialist cabinet in the meantime.
The Socialist prime minister-designate Nikolai Dobrev presented a short-term programme for his planned government to the Socialist leadership two days ago.

It included economic stabilisation measures based on IMF recommendations like implementing a currency board mechanism, stabilising collapsing banks, improving tax revenue and closing loss-making state firms.
Economic analysts said that the plan was the opposite of what the Socialists have been doing in the past two years, since they came to power in 1994.
"Who will believe them now?" said one analyst.
The UDF, whose early election calls are backed by Stoyanov, says an interim government backed by all political forces has the constitutional power to negotiate with multilateral lenders.
"The BSP is incapable of implementing an anti-crisis programme alone," Kostov said.
Speeding up structural reform, drafting of a realistic 1997 budget and seeking humanitarian aid from the European Union are also part of the UDF package, said Kostov.
